title: Distribution-Sensitive Bounds on Relative Approximations of Geometric Ranges
abstract:
A family R of ranges and a set X of points, all in R^d, together define a range space (X, R|_X), where R|_X = {X cap h | h in R}. We want to find a structure to estimate the quantity |X cap h|/|X| for any range h in R with the (rho, epsilon)-guarantee: (i) if |X cap h|/|X| > rho, the estimate must have a relative error epsilon; (ii) otherwise, the estimate must have an absolute error rho epsilon. The objective is to minimize the size of the structure. Currently, the dominant solution is to compute a relative (rho, epsilon)-approximation, which is a subset of X with O~(lambda/(rho epsilon^2)) points, where lambda is the VC-dimension of (X, R|_X), and O~ hides polylog factors.
This paper shows a more general bound sensitive to the content of X. We give a structure that stores O(log (1/rho)) integers plus O~(theta * (lambda/epsilon^2)) points of X, where theta - called the disagreement coefficient - measures how much the ranges differ from each other in their intersections with X. The value of theta is between 1 and 1/rho, such that our space bound is never worse than that of relative (rho, epsilon)-approximations, but we improve the latter’s 1/rho term whenever theta = o(1/(rho log (1/rho))). We also prove that, in the worst case, summaries with the (rho, 1/2)-guarantee must consume Omega(theta) words even for d = 2 and lambda <=3.
We then constrain R to be the set of halfspaces in R^d for a constant d, and prove the existence of structures with o(1/(rho epsilon^2)) size offering (rho,epsilon)-guarantees, when X is generated from various stochastic distributions. This is the first formal justification on why the term 1/rho is not compulsory for "realistic" inputs.

      Abstract
A family R of ranges and a set X of points, all in Rd , together define a range space (X, R|X ), where
R|X = {X ∩ h | h ∈ R}. We want to find a structure to estimate the quantity |X ∩ h|/|X| for any
range h ∈ R with the (ρ, )-guarantee: (i) if |X ∩ h|/|X| > ρ, the estimate must have a relative error
; (ii) otherwise, the estimate must have an absolute error ρ. The objective is to minimize the size
of the structure. Currently, the dominant solution is to compute a relative (ρ, )-approximation,
which is a subset of X with Õ(λ/(ρ2 )) points, where λ is the VC-dimension of (X, R|X ), and Õ
hides polylog factors.
     This paper shows a more general bound sensitive to the content of X. We give a structure
that stores O(log(1/ρ)) integers plus Õ(θ · (λ/2 )) points of X, where θ – called the disagreement
coefficient – measures how much the ranges differ from each other in their intersections with X.
The value of θ is between 1 and 1/ρ, such that our space bound is never worse than that of relative

(ρ, )-approximations, but we improve the latter’s 1/ρ term whenever θ = o( ρ log(1/ρ) ). We also prove
that, in the worst case, summaries with the (ρ, 1/2)-guarantee must consume Ω(θ) words even for
d = 2 and λ ≤ 3.
     We then constrain R to be the set of halfspaces in Rd for a constant d, and prove the existence of
structures with o(1/(ρ2 )) size offering (ρ, )-guarantees, when X is generated from various stochastic
distributions. This is the first formal justification on why the term 1/ρ is not compulsory for
“realistic” inputs.

 1      Introduction
A (data) summary, in general, refers to a structure that captures certain information up
to a specified precision about a set of objects, but using space significantly smaller than
the size of the set. These summaries have become important tools in algorithm design,
especially in distributed/parallel computing where the main performance goal is to minimize
the communication across different servers.
    In this paper, we revisit the problem of finding a small-space summary to perform range
estimation in Rd with relative-error guarantees. Let R be a family of geometric ranges in Rd
(e.g., a “halfspace family” R is the set of all halfspaces in Rd ), and X be a set of points in Rd .
R and X together define a range space (X, R|X ), where R|X = {X ∩ h | h ∈ R}. Denote by
λ the VC-dimension of (X, R|X ).

       1.1     Previous results
       Throughout the paper, all logarithms have base 2 by default.

       1.1.1     Sample-Based (ρ, )-Summaries
       We say that a (ρ, )-summary of (X, R|X ) is sample-based if it meets the requirements below:
       it stores a subset Z ⊆ X such that, for any range h ∈ R with Z ∩ h = ∅, it returns an
       estimate 0 for X(h).

        · max{ρ, X(h)} holds for all ranges h ∈ R. Hence, the (ρ, )-guarantee can be fulfilled by
       simply setting τ to Z(h), rendering Z a legal (sample-based) (ρ, )-summary. Strengthening
       earlier results [3, 12, 21], Li et al. [17] proved that a random sample of X with size O( ρ1 ·

       1.1.2     A Lower Bound of Ω(1/ρ)
       Notice that all the above bounds contain a term 1/ρ. This is not a coincidence, but instead
       is due to a connection to “-nets”. Given a range space (X, R|X ), an -net [13] is a subset
       Z ⊆ X such that Z(h) > 0 holds for any range h ∈ R satisfying X(h) ≥ . As can be verified
       easily, any sample-based (ρ, 1/2)-summary of (X, R|X ) must also be a ρ-net. This implies
       that the smallest size of sample-based (ρ, 1/2)-summaries must be at least that of ρ-nets.
           Regarding the sizes of -nets, a lower bound of Ω( 1 log 1 ) is known for many range families
       R (see [14, 15, 20] and the references therein). More precisely, this means that, for each such
       family R, one cannot hope to obtain an -net of size o( 1 log 1 ) for every possible X. It thus

follows that, for these families R, Ω( ρ1 log ρ1 ) is a lower bound on the sizes of sample-based
(ρ, 1/2)-summaries. This, in turn, indicates that range spaces (X, R|X ) defined by such an
R cannot always be well-behaved.
     Coming back to the sizes of -nets, a weaker lower bound of Ω(1/) holds quite commonly
even on the range families that evade the Ω( 1 log 1 ) bound. Consider, for example, the
halfspace family R in R2 . For any X, the range space (X, R|X ) definitely has an -net of
size O(1/) [10, 19]. This is tight: place a set X of points on the boundary of a circle; and it
is easy to show that any -net of (X, R|X ) must have a size of at least 1/. This means that
the size of any sample-based (ρ, 1/2)-summary of (X, R|X ) must be Ω(1/ρ).


1.2     Our results
1.2.1    On One Input: Moving Beyond Ω(1/ρ)
The Ω(1/ρ) lower bound discussed earlier holds only in the worst case, i.e., it is determined
by the “hardest” X. For other X, the range space (X, R|X ) may admit much smaller
(ρ, )-summaries. For example, let R be again the set of halfplanes in R2 . When all the points
of X lie on a line, (X, R) has a sample-based (ρ, )-approximation of size only O( 1 log ρ1 );
also, it would be interesting to note that (X, R) has an -net that contains only 2 points! In
general, the existing bounds on (ρ, )-summaries can be excessively loose on individual inputs
X. This calls for an alternative, distribution-sensitive, analytical framework that is able to
prove tighter bounds using extra complexity parameters that depend on the content of X.
     The first contribution of this paper is to establish such a framework by resorting to the
concept of disagreement coefficient [8] from active learning. This notion was originally defined
in a context different from ours; and we will adapt it to range spaces in the next section.
At this moment, it suffices to understand that the disagreement coefficient θ is a real value
satisfying: 1 ≤ θ ≤ 1/ρ. The coefficient quantifies the differences among the sets in R|X
(a larger θ indicates greater differences). Even under the same R, θ may vary considerably
depending on X.
     We will show that, for any range space (X, R|X ) of VC-dimension λ, there is a (ρ, )-
summary that keeps O(log(1/ρ)) integers plus

a (ρ, 1/2)-summary even when d = 2 and λ ≤ 3. This generalizes the Ω(1/ρ) lower bound

1.2.2    On a Distribution of Inputs: Small Summaries for Halfspaces
Our framework allows us to explain – for the first time we believe – why Ω(1/ρ) · poly(1/)
is too pessimistic a bound on the sizes of (ρ, )-summaries for inputs encountered in practice.
For this purpose, we must not allow arbitrary inputs because of the prevalent Ω(1/ρ) lower
bound; instead, we will examine a class of inputs following a certain distribution.

 2       Disagreement coefficients

2.1      Existing Definitions on Distributions
Disagreement coefficient was introduced by Hanneke [8] to analyze active learning algorithms
(although a similar concept had been coined earlier [1] in statistics).
    Let D be a distribution over Rd . For any region A ⊆ Rd , we denote by PrD [A] the
probability of x ∈ A when x is drawn from D. Let R be a family of geometric ranges. Given
a subset R0 ⊆ R, define the disagreement region DIS(R0 ) of R0 as

      DIS(R0 )   =   {x ∈ Rd | ∃h1 , h2 ∈ R0 s.t. x ∈ h1 and x ∈
                                                               / h2 }.

That is, DIS(R0 ) includes every such point x ∈ Rd that does not fall in all the ranges in R0 ,
and in the meantime, does not fall outside all the ranges in R0 , either. Given a range h ∈ R
and a real value r > 0, define its r-ball BD (h, r) as the set of all ranges h0 ∈ R satisfying
PrD [DIS({h, h0 })] ≤ r. It is worth mentioning that DIS({h, h0 }) is simply the symmetric
difference between h and h0 .
